title: SRE SLOs, Error Budgets, Capacity Planning, Reliability Initiatives, and Runbooks
author: Ari Chen
content:
Overview

This document consolidates Redwood Inference's SRE guidance for defining and operating Service Level Objectives (SLOs), managing error budgets, conducting capacity planning, running reliability initiatives, standardizing incident reviews, maintaining operational tooling, and authoring runbooks. It is intended for service owners, SREs, on-call engineers, and engineering managers.

Scope

- Applies to production-facing services that are part of the Redwood inference platform including: serving-runtime, routing-service, kv-cache, batch-scheduler, metrics-collector, and control-plane.
- Includes cross-region and dedicated/private deployment considerations.

Definitions

- SLI (Service Level Indicator): A measurable signal of user-perceived reliability (latency, availability, correctness).
- SLO (Service Level Objective): Target on an SLI (e.g., 99.95% success over 30d).
- Error budget: 1 - SLO; the allowable unreliability over a rolling window.
- Burn rate: Speed at which error budget is being consumed.

Principles

1. Customer-centric SLIs: measure what impacts customers (tail latency, correct responses, API errors).
2. Simple, actionable SLOs: avoid dozens of overlapping targets per service - prefer a small set of high-signal SLOs.
3. Ownership and accountability: every SLO must have a single owner and documented mitigation/playbook.
4. Automated measurement and alerting: SLOs and burn rates are automatically computed and visible in dashboards.
5. Use error budgets to drive trade-offs (deployments, feature rollouts, on-call load).

SLO Catalog (recommended canonical SLOs)

| Service | SLI | SLO (30d rolling) | Rationale | Owner |
|---|---:|---:|---|---|
| serving-runtime | request success (2xx) | 99.95% | Primary availability for customer inference requests | eng-serving-runtime
| serving-runtime | p95 latency (inference payload) | <200ms | Low-latency SLAs for interactive features | eng-serving-runtime
| routing-service | request success | 99.99% | Routing is critical for request delivery and model fallbacks | eng-platform
| kv-cache | cache-hit rate | >=85% | Reduces cost and latency for repeated prefixes | eng-serving-runtime
| control-plane | CRUD ops success | 99.9% | Customer-facing control plane operations | eng-platform

Error Budget Policy

- Window: 30-day rolling window (default). Some infra primitives may additionally track 7-day windows for rapid response.
- Burn rate thresholds trigger actions:
  1. Low (burn rate < 2x): Continue normal ops; inform PM/owner in weekly report.
  2. Elevated (2x <= burn rate < 5x): Owner investigates within 24 hours; freeze non-critical deploys to the service.
  3. Critical (burn rate >= 5x): Immediate mitigation required; page SRE on-call and follow incident/mitigation runbook.

- Deploy policy tied to budgets: When error budget remaining < 25%, all non-essential feature rollouts to the service are halted; CI merges that modify core paths require SRE approval.

Monitoring, Alerting, and Dashboards

- Canonical dashboards (Grafana): per-service SLO panel, burn rate, request volume, p50/p95/p99 latency, error breakdown by code, and top caller services.
- Alerts:
  - SLO burn rate page: fire when burn rate > 2x for 30m; severity: P2.
  - SLO remaining < 25%: notify owner + eng manager (P3).
  - SLO remaining < 10%: page SRE on-call + owner (P1).

- Example Prometheus query snippets (replace service=\"serving-runtime\"):
  - Success rate (30d):
    sum(rate(http_requests_total{service=\"serving-runtime\",code=~\"2..\"}[30d])) / sum(rate(http_requests_total{service=\"serving-runtime\"}[30d]))
  - p95 latency (5m window):
    histogram_quantile(0.95, sum(rate(http_request_duration_seconds_bucket{service=\"serving-runtime\"}[5m])) by (le))

Capacity Planning (process + thresholds)

Purpose: ensure capacity meets SLOs during expected traffic and planned growth while minimizing cost.

Process (quarterly, with monthly checks):
1. Forecast demand: combine historical traffic, product roadmaps, upcoming promotions, and customer commit changes.
2. Run stress simulations in staging with representative request patterns and model sizes.
3. Define safety buffer: production target = 95th percentile required capacity + 20% buffer for transient bursts.
4. Capacity purchases and allocation: schedule Dedicated pool changes and commit reservations 30-60 days ahead for large capacity changes.
5. Validate post-change: run Canary (10-20% traffic) and monitor SLOs for 24-72 hours before full rollout.

Capacity thresholds (example):
- Scale-up threshold: CPU/GPU utilization sustained > 75% for > 10 min AND request queue length > 50.
- Scale-down threshold: utilization < 40% for > 20 min AND queue length < 10.
- Queue length acceptable per serving node: <= 100 concurrent requests in-flight.

Operational Tooling for SREs

- Dashboards: Grafana SLO pages, per-service runbook quick-links, and topology maps.
- Playbook runner: central runbook system with checklists, auto-checks (API health, dependency status), and one-click paging.
- Alert router: SREAlert (internal) routes pages based on service ownership, severity, and on-call schedule.
- Cost/capacity tools: a capacity-forecast spreadsheet + automated cost simulation that models batching/quantization changes.

Reliability Initiatives and Project Lifecycle

- Initiative intake: reliability projects are proposed via PRD-lite with impact, risk, owners, and measurement plan.
- Prioritization: initiatives ranked by customer impact x probability of success / engineering cost.
- Common initiative types: autoscaling improvements, caching optimizations, kernel-level performance fixes, model-variant fallbacks, and improved tracing.
- Measurement: each initiative must declare success criteria (SLO improvement, cost reduction, or latency reduction) and a 90/10 rollback plan.

Incident Review Standards (postmortems)

Every Sev2/Sev1 incident must produce a postmortem within 72 hours and be updated to final form within 7 days. Postmortem template (must include these headings):
1. Summary: short paragraph with impact and timeline.
2. Detection: how and when was the incident detected (monitoring/alert/customer report).
3. Impact: services, customers, regions impacted, and mitigation timeline.
4. Root cause analysis: clear causal chain (avoid root-cause-of-root-cause).
5. Action items: owner, type (preventive/operational), priority, ETA.
6. Follow-ups: tracking in backlog with links.
7. Learnings: what changed in processes or tooling.
8. SLO/ERR budget impact: quantify consumed error budget and changes to thresholds if any.

Action item policy: at least one preventive engineering task for Sev1 incidents; must be scheduled or assigned in JIRA within 7 days.

Runbooks (canonical examples)

A. High client-facing p95 latency (serving-runtime)
1. Triage: check Grafana SLO panel and top-level latency heatmap.
2. Top 5 checks (fast):
   - Verify cluster GPU utilization: kubectl top nodes (or cloud GPU console).
   - Check recent deployments (last 60m): gitops/CI pipeline history.
   - Inspect request error rates and codes: query traces for 5xx spikes.
   - Validate KV cache hit rate: dashboard panel.
   - Look for throttling from routing-service: \"RateLimit\" logs.
3. Mitigation (ordered):
   - If a recent deploy correlates with spike: rollback to previous model/service.
     CLI: argocd app rollback serving-runtime --rev <previous>
   - If GPU saturation: scale up nodepool by +20% or move hot-models to dedicated pool.
     Example (GKE): gcloud container clusters resize <cluster> --node-pool=<pool> --num-nodes=<n>
   - If cache-hit drop: flush warm cache and re-prime for top prefixes; increase cache memory in KV nodes.
4. Post-incident: create JIRA linking to postmortem; update SLO dashboard if measurement bug found.

B. Model inference OOMs / worker OOM (serving-runtime)
1. Detect: look for OOM logs, OOMKill in systemd or kernel messages.
2. Immediate actions: lower max batch size via runtime feature flag, restart affected replicas.
   - Example CLI to change config: curl -X PATCH https://control-plane/api/configs/serving-runtime -d '{"max_batch_size":128}' -H 'Authorization: Bearer <token>'
3. If widespread: rollback recent quantization/compilation changes; reboot nodes with healthy kernel.
4. Long term: add pre-deploy memory pressure tests and GPU heap monitoring.

C. Routing-service 5xx spike
1. Check service health endpoints and circuit-breaker state.
2. Isolate problematic downstream (eg. serving-runtime region variant) and switch to fallback route.
   - Example: update route weight to fallback model: curl -X POST https://control-plane/api/routes/<route-id>/weights -d '{"fallback":0.8}'
3. If DB/metadata store is degraded: promote read replica or failover following DB runbook.

Escalation and On-call Roles

- First responder: service owner on-call.
- SRE on-call: pages for burn-rate-critical or infrastructure-wide degradation.
- Engineering manager: pages for business-impacting incidents > 60 minutes or sustained budget depletion.

Governance and Review Cadence

- Quarterly SLO review: owners validate SLOs, SLIs, and thresholds; retire or add SLOs as business needs change.
- Monthly capacity sync: infra + product + SRE to review forecasts and upcoming events.
- Postmortem review: weekly postmortem review meeting where high-severity incident owners present findings and action plans.

Templates and Example Snippets

- Example SLO YAML snippet (used by SLO service):

  name: serving-runtime-success-rate
  service: serving-runtime
  sli: http_success_rate
  window_days: \"30\"
  objective: \"99.95\"
  measurement_query: \"sum(rate(http_requests_total{service=\\\"serving-runtime\\\",code=~\\\"2..\\\"}[30d])) / sum(rate(http_requests_total{service=\\\"serving-runtime\\\"}[30d]))\"

- Incident postmortem checklist (JIRA template):
  - Summary
  - Detection time & source
  - Timeline (5-10 minute granularity for first 2 hours)
  - Root cause and causal chain
  - Customer impact quantification
  - Action items with owners & due dates
